title: Saudi Arabia still views the US as its main strategic partner – despite Trump’s nuclear agreement conditions
gist: Chatham House reads a cluster of late-July 2026 events – a 22 July US–Saudi civilian nuclear agreement, Houthi attacks on Aramco's Red Sea export hubs, a 43-country maritime coalition summit in Riyadh, and joint Saudi-US airstrikes in eastern Iraq – as one deliberate Saudi strategy: build indispensability to Washington through regional security provision so that the partnership is no longer conditioned on normalizing with Israel. Riyadh will not join the Abraham Accords absent progress on Palestinian statehood, and is instead competing with the UAE for US favour on a broader security-and-energy basis.

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia has shifted its strategic objective from securing US protection to safeguarding its own interests in a region where US engagement is still substantial but far less predictable, meaning Riyadh now behaves as a security provider rather than a security consumer.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Reprices Gulf risk: Saudi policy decisions (defence spend, coalition-building, unilateral strikes) become an independent variable rather than a derivative of US posture.
insights.quote: The challenge for Riyadh is no longer how to secure US protection. It is how to safeguard Saudi interests in a region where US engagement remains substantial, but is less predictable than in the past.
insights.locator: This is not simply a response to President

insights.claim: President Trump's war against Iran – described as the largest deployment of US forces since 1990 – is what pushed Riyadh to reassess its role in the regional order, an ironic outcome given a decade of US efforts to reduce Middle East exposure.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The escalation that was meant to shrink US commitments has instead deepened Gulf-US operational entanglement — watch for sustained elevated defence and force-posture spending.
insights.quote: it is President Donald Trump’s war against Iran – involving the largest deployment of US forces since 1990 – that has prompted Riyadh to reassess its role in the regional order
insights.locator: Ironically, it is President Donald Trump’s war

insights.claim: Chatham House flags that unilateral actions by Israel or Iran can trigger wider instability that directly hits Saudi interests, making Riyadh a hostage to two actors it does not control.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Tail risk to Gulf energy assets is exogenous to Saudi policy — hedges should key off Israeli/Iranian escalation, not Saudi restraint.
insights.locator: Recent conflicts have also reinforced the risks

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia and the US signed a civilian nuclear agreement on 22 July 2026 that establishes a framework for long-term cooperation and positions US companies to play a leading role in the Saudi nuclear programme.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A multi-decade addressable market for US nuclear engineering, fuel-cycle and EPC vendors opens — subject to congressional/approval risk described below.

insights.claim: Riyadh deliberately held out for a nuclear deal with Washington rather than accepting alternatives from Moscow or Beijing, revealing that its default preference for US technology, expertise and investment survived a decade of talk about Gulf hedging toward Russia and China.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'Gulf is pivoting to China' narrative in the highest-value technology tie-ups; favours US over Russian/Chinese nuclear vendors in Gulf tenders.
insights.quote: The agreement represents the culmination of years of patient negotiation by Riyadh, as it persisted in seeking a deal with Washington – rather than Moscow or Beijing.

insights.claim: One day after the 22 July signing, President Trump sought to link approval of the US–Saudi nuclear agreement to Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords and normalizing relations with Israel — creating explicit execution risk over an already-signed deal.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Signed does not mean approved: companies pricing in Saudi nuclear revenue face a political gate that Riyadh has publicly refused to pass through.
insights.locator: However, one day after it was signed

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia has consistently maintained that formal relations with Israel depend on meaningful progress towards Palestinian statehood, and that position has hardened rather than softened following the war in Gaza and the anger it generated across the Arab world.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Bets on near-term Saudi-Israel normalization — and the asset repricing that would follow — are unlikely to pay; the constraint is domestic and regional legitimacy, not negotiation.
insights.quote: Saudi Arabia has consistently maintained that formal relations with Israel depend on meaningful progress towards Palestinian statehood.

insights.claim: Mohammed bin Salman is arguing that Saudi contributions to regional stability, economic security and collective security should earn progress in the bilateral relationship without further conditions, which Chatham House characterises as 'politically impossible' ones like joining the Abraham Accords.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Frames the bargaining chip Riyadh will actually trade — security services and coalition leadership, not recognition of Israel.
insights.quote: particularly politically impossible ones like joining the Abraham Accords

themes.theme: Red Sea chokepoint and Aramco export vulnerability

insights.claim: The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz has raised the strategic importance of the Red Sea as an alternative route for energy exports and international trade, concentrating risk on a second chokepoint rather than diversifying it away.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Both major Gulf export routes are now contested simultaneously — freight and war-risk insurance premia and tanker rates have structurally higher floors.

insights.claim: On 20 July the Iran-backed Houthi militia announced a blockade of Saudi-linked shipping through the Bab al-Mandab Strait and within days claimed attacks against Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, marking a shift from targeting Israeli-linked traffic to targeting Saudi assets directly.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Saudi-flagged/linked tonnage now carries a specific risk premium; watch rerouting around the Cape and its effect on tanker tonne-miles.
insights.locator: But in recent days the Iran-backed Houthi militia

insights.claim: On 25 July the Houthis launched missile and drone strikes against Aramco facilities in Jizan and Yanbu, Saudi Arabia's principal Red Sea oil export hub, taking the conflict directly onto Saudi export infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Direct physical risk to Saudi crude and refined product export capacity on the Red Sea coast — a supply-disruption catalyst distinct from Hormuz.
insights.locator: On 25 July, it launched missile and drone strikes

insights.claim: The Houthi campaign has exposed a significant vulnerability for the kingdom and the wider global economy, raising commercial shipping costs and prompting concerns about the resilience of international supply chains and energy markets.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Second-order inflation channel: sustained chokepoint disruption feeds freight and energy costs into global goods prices.
insights.locator: These moves have exposed a significant vulnerability

insights.claim: On 30 July Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Defence convened military chiefs and representatives from 43 countries plus the European Union in Riyadh to discuss establishing a new maritime security coalition to defend freedom of navigation in the Red Sea.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A Saudi-hosted naval coalition would be the first Gulf-led answer to Red Sea disruption — track its formation as the key variable for shipping risk normalization.
insights.locator: The Saudi government has stepped up

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia offered to host the coalition's headquarters and secured the support of only 14 of the 43 participating states, a modest conversion rate that Chatham House nevertheless reads as the clearest signal yet of Riyadh's willingness to lead collective security responses.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The gap between attendees (43) and committed backers (14) is the real measure of how fast Red Sea protection can be stood up.
insights.locator: The kingdom proposed to host the coalition’s headquarters

themes.theme: Joint kinetic action against Iran-aligned groups

insights.claim: Joint Saudi-US precision airstrikes on 28 July hit Iran-aligned groups in eastern Iraq after those groups directed more than 30 drone attacks at Saudi energy infrastructure and US forces within a 72-hour period.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A 30-plus-drone salvo in three days against energy assets is a step-change in attack tempo — the relevant metric for pricing Gulf supply risk.
insights.locator: The joint Saudi-US airstrikes of 28 July

insights.claim: The strikes broke Saudi Arabia's long-standing avoidance of direct military action inside Iraq, and came despite several years of Riyadh deliberately reducing tensions with Tehran — signalling that de-escalation policy will not restrain retaliation when Saudi security interests are hit directly.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Saudi-Iran détente is no longer a reliable ceiling on escalation; escalation scenarios need a higher base rate.
insights.quote: By acting alongside the US , Riyadh signalled that its pursuit of regional de-escalation does not preclude a willingness to respond when its security interests are directly challenged.
insights.locator: The operation was notable not only because

themes.theme: Gulf competition with the UAE for US favour

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia's recent activism has a competitive dimension aimed at the UAE, which has already normalized with Israel via the Abraham Accords and enjoys a close relationship with the Trump administration — so Riyadh is substituting security value for the normalization card it will not play.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Intra-Gulf competition for US attention becomes a driver of Saudi defence, maritime and energy-infrastructure commitments — read Saudi announcements as bids, not just policy.
insights.locator: There is also, notably, a competitive dimension

insights.claim: By leading on regional security, maritime security and energy flows, Riyadh is deliberately broadening the basis of its value to Washington beyond trade and investment alone, arguing for a partnership defined by shared interests rather than a single political objective.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect Saudi headline investment pledges to be accompanied — and increasingly replaced — by security deliverables as the currency of the relationship.
insights.quote: Riyadh is making the case for a partnership defined by shared interests rather than a single political objective.
